prompt: A page written for a telephone line loads today over fibre, unchanged. What allows that?
hint: Ask what each layer is permitted to know about the others.

choices.text: The browser detects what the connection is made of and picks a version of the protocol to suit it
choices.why: Nothing in a browser inspects the medium; it would have no way to and no reason to.

choices.text: The layer that carries was never allowed to know what the layer above means
choices.why: Change the bottom and the top does not notice, because it was never told.

choices.text: Fibre was designed to accept the signals a telephone line accepted
choices.why: The signals are entirely different; the compatibility is higher up.

choices.text: The router converts the page before handing it to the machine that asked
choices.why: A router does not open the page, which is the point of the arrangement.

prompt: Eight programs and five ways of carrying, with no layer in between. How many pieces of work?
hint: Each program would need its own version for each medium.

choices.text: Thirteen, because each side has to learn the one thing in the middle and needs no more
choices.why: Thirteen is the count once a layer exists between them. This question removes it.

choices.text: Forty
choices.why: Eight times five: every pairing written by hand.

choices.text: Eight, one for each program, since the medium is handled underneath
choices.why: Handled underneath by what? The question removes the thing that would do it.

choices.text: Five, one for each medium, which the programs then share between them
choices.why: Sharing is what a layer is. Without one there is nothing to share.

prompt: Fill the blank: many protocols above, many technologies below, one mandatory layer in the middle — that shape is called the narrow ___.
hint: It is the thin part of an hourglass.

prompt: Which of these are real costs of layering? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three of them are paid on every packet or by somebody downstream.

choices.text: Header bytes, which are paid whether or not you sent much content
choices.why: A fixed overhead, and most of the traffic when the messages are small.

choices.text: A handover at every boundary, performed for every packet of every connection
choices.why: Small individually, and the reason a busy device runs warm.

choices.text: A layer guessing about something its neighbour knows and it cannot see
choices.why: Loss on Wi-Fi is the standard example.

choices.text: The message being rewritten from scratch at each hop along the way
choices.why: The message is wrapped, not rewritten. Only the outermost wrap is rebuilt.

choices.text: A ceiling on how many programs one machine can have talking at once
choices.why: That limit comes from ports and memory, and is unrelated to layering.

prompt: On Wi-Fi, TCP slows down when a packet goes missing. When is that the wrong response?
hint: Ask what caused the loss, and whether going slower addresses it.

choices.text: Wi-Fi is generally quicker than the wired networks the rule was written for, so the reduction is applied to a number that was already high enough
choices.why: Speed is not what the rule reacts to; loss is.

choices.text: Slowing down puts more packets in flight at once, which makes the loss worse
choices.why: It puts fewer in flight. The direction here is backwards.

choices.text: When the loss was interference, which is not reduced by sending less
choices.why: A microwave oven is indifferent to how politely you transmit.

choices.text: When the router has already asked for the packet again on transport's behalf
choices.why: A router does not retransmit for you; it has not opened the segment.

prompt: Somebody describes a device as a layer 2 switch. What does the number tell you?
hint: The number is about how far up it reads.

choices.text: It reads as far as MAC addresses and carries everything above them unopened
choices.why: That is the whole content of the label: where it stops looking.

choices.text: It has two network sockets, which is where the number in the name comes from
choices.why: Switches have many sockets, and the number is not a count of them.

choices.text: It handles two protocols at once, one for addresses and one for ports
choices.why: Ports belong to a layer above the one this device reads.

choices.text: It is the second device a frame meets on its way out of the building
choices.why: The number names a layer, not a position along the path.

prompt: Match each layer to the question it answers.
hint: Read them from the bottom of the stack upwards.

pairs.right: What is a one, in voltage or light?
Which card, on this particular wire?
Which machine, and by which route?

right_distractors: What does this message actually mean?
How are these bytes written down?

prompt: Why are layers 5 and 6 difficult to point at in a stack that is running?
hint: Ask who does those jobs in practice.

choices.text: They were dropped in a later revision and survive in older teaching material alone
choices.why: They were not dropped. They are in the model and hard to locate in the traffic.

choices.text: They run on the server side alone, so a browser has no counterpart to them
choices.why: Both ends of a connection are described by the same model.

choices.text: The jobs are done, but by TLS or by the application rather than by layers of their own
choices.why: Real work, no separate box, which is why people argue about where to draw it.

choices.text: They were folded into layer 4 at the point where transport took over encryption
choices.why: Transport did not take over encryption; TLS sits beside the boundary.

prompt: Fill the blank: a load balancer that chooses a server by looking at the request path has to read up to layer ___.
hint: The topmost of the seven.

prompt: A team wants `/api/` sent to one group of servers and everything else to another. What does that need?
hint: Ask what has to be read before the decision can be made.

choices.text: A balancer at layer 4, which is cheaper and looks at the port the connection arrived on
choices.why: A port cannot tell `/api/` from anything else; both arrive on 443.

choices.text: A second public address, with one group of servers behind each
choices.why: That works by making the client choose, which was not the arrangement asked for.

choices.text: A balancer that reads the request, and therefore holds the certificate
choices.why: Reading the path means decrypting, and decrypting means holding the key.

choices.text: A change to the address of each server, so the path is decided by routing
choices.why: Routing decides on addresses; the path is not one.

prompt: Which of the seven layers were folded into the single link layer of the four?
hint: The bottom two.

choices.text: Session, presentation and application, because a program settles its own encoding
choices.why: Those three were folded, but into the application layer at the top.

choices.text: Physical and data link
choices.why: Both are decided together by whoever designed the medium.

choices.text: Network and data link, since both of them are about addresses
choices.why: They are about different addresses, and the model keeps them apart.

choices.text: Physical alone; the data link layer kept a layer of its own
choices.why: The four-layer model has no separate data link layer.

prompt: Why is UDP a reasonable choice for carrying a voice call?
hint: Ask what a late syllable is worth.

choices.text: It hands over each piece in the order it was sent, which matters more in a conversation than it does for a page
choices.why: Ordering is TCP's promise. UDP makes no such offer.

choices.text: It reserves bandwidth along the path in advance, which keeps the call steady
choices.why: Nothing about UDP reserves anything; it sends and stops.

choices.text: Its headers carry timing information that TCP leaves out
choices.why: Timing is added by the protocol above, not by UDP itself.

choices.text: A syllable that arrives late is useless, so waiting for it buys nothing
choices.why: For anything live, late and lost amount to the same thing.

prompt: Which of these are true of the four-layer model? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about what it specifies and what it declines to.

choices.text: Its two middle layers line up one to one with two of the seven
choices.why: Transport and network match; the ends are where the models differ.

choices.text: It leaves what a wire is made of to whoever built the wire
choices.why: It says put it on the wire and specifies no further.

choices.text: It arrived with working code that universities could copy for nothing
choices.why: That, more than the design, is why it spread.

choices.text: It was published first, and the seven-layer model was written as a reply to it
choices.why: The two were developed in parallel; neither is a reply to the other.

choices.text: It adds a layer for encryption that the seven-layer model lacks
choices.why: It has no encryption layer at all, which is why TLS has no number.

prompt: Fill the blank: a DNS lookup is one small question and one small answer, so it is normally carried over ___ rather than over a protocol that sets up a connection first.
hint: Three letters, and it sends without agreeing first.

prompt: Which of these best explains why TCP/IP became the stack everybody runs?
hint: Three practical reasons and one about the design.

choices.text: It had the backing of an international standards body, with a published document covering each of its layers
choices.why: That describes the model it beat, and the backing did not decide it.

choices.text: It described each layer in more detail, which left less to argue about
choices.why: It described less, which is what left less to argue about.

choices.text: It was faster on the hardware of the period by a wide margin
choices.why: Speed was not the deciding difference between the two.

choices.text: It was already running, free to copy, and specified less
choices.why: Working code in an operating system people already had.

prompt: Who is a TCP header written for?
hint: A header is a note to a counterpart, not to a neighbour.

choices.text: Each router along the way, which reads the port number to decide where the packet goes next
choices.why: Routers decide on addresses and do not open the segment at all.

choices.text: The transport layer at the far end
choices.why: Each header is addressed to the same layer on the other machine.

choices.text: The internet layer just below it, which needs the ports to build its own header
choices.why: The internet layer needs addresses, and gets them from elsewhere.

choices.text: The program that receives the message, which reads it before the content
choices.why: The program is handed a stream; the header was consumed below it.

prompt: Put the four wraps in the order they are added on the way out.
hint: Start with what the program wrote.
items: The application's bytes, with nothing around them
A transport header in front, carrying the ports
An internet header in front of that, carrying the addresses
A link header in front, and a check behind
trap: The tempting mistake is starting at the link layer, because it is what reaches the wire first. It is added last and read first, which is the same fact seen from two ends.

prompt: Fill the blank: transport produces a segment, the internet layer produces a packet, and what goes onto the wire is a ___.
hint: It is the one with MAC addresses on it.

prompt: What is thrown away and rebuilt at every hop?
hint: Ask which envelope was only ever addressed to the next card.

choices.text: The transport header, because each router recalculates its checksum over the new addresses
choices.why: No router opens the transport header, so none recalculates anything in it.

choices.text: The frame
choices.why: It was addressed to one card on one wire, and is finished once it crosses.

choices.text: The packet's addresses, which are set to the next router each time
choices.why: Those addresses are the point of the packet and survive the whole trip.

choices.text: The same bytes travel from end to end, untouched by the routers
choices.why: The outermost envelope is rebuilt at every hop, so something changes.

prompt: A forty-byte request gains a twenty-byte transport header, a twenty-byte internet header, a fourteen-byte link header and a four-byte check at the end. How many bytes go onto the wire?
hint: Add the four wraps to what the application wrote.

prompt: A page loads over Wi-Fi at home and over a mobile network on the train, with no change to the browser. Which rule is doing the work?
hint: Two rules were named. This is the one about who talks to whom.

choices.text: The browser detects the connection and selects a protocol version to match it
choices.why: The browser is not consulted about what the bottom of the stack is made of.

choices.text: Wi-Fi and mobile networks agreed on one shared frame format for this purpose
choices.why: Their frames differ considerably; the sameness is further up.

choices.text: A layer talks only to its neighbours, so the top is not told what the bottom is
choices.why: The application layer is not entitled to an opinion about the medium.

choices.text: The operating system translates between the two before the browser is involved
choices.why: There is nothing to translate: the browser hands down the same bytes either way.

prompt: NAT rewrites a port number. Which rule does that break, and who ends up paying?
hint: A port belongs to a layer above the box doing the rewriting.

choices.text: It puts a second address into the packet, so the machine behind it has two at once and the server sees both
choices.why: There is one address in the packet at any point; NAT replaces it rather than adding.

choices.text: It changes the hop count, so a trace shows fewer routers than were crossed
choices.why: Every router changes the hop count; that is its ordinary use.

choices.text: It reads the request path, which is why it has to hold the certificate
choices.why: NAT does not read the path. That is a layer 7 balancer.

choices.text: It opens a header addressed to somebody else, and new protocols pay for it later
choices.why: Boxes that assumed a shape drop what does not have it, years afterwards.

prompt: Match each thing to the layer that wrote it.
hint: One of them is written by the program itself.

prompt: Fill the blank: the hop count falls by one at each router so that a packet caught in a ___ eventually dies instead of circling for ever.
hint: It goes round and comes back.

prompt: A router between you and a server does which of these? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask how far up it reads before deciding.

choices.text: Discards the frame it received
choices.why: That frame was only ever good for the wire it arrived on.

choices.text: Reads the destination address in the packet
choices.why: That is the decision it exists to make.

choices.text: Builds a fresh frame for the next wire
choices.why: New addresses, and possibly a different medium entirely.

choices.text: Puts the segments back into order before passing them on
choices.why: Reordering happens at the far end; a router has not opened the segment.

choices.text: Checks that the request is one the destination server will accept
choices.why: It has no idea what a request is, and would have to read four layers up.

prompt: Two networks cannot reach each other, and somebody suggests a switch. Why is it the wrong box?
hint: Ask where a switch stops reading.

choices.text: A switch forwards what it receives to each socket in turn, which would flood both networks
choices.why: A switch learns which card is where; flooding is what it stops doing.

choices.text: It stops at MAC addresses, and reaching another network is decided above them
choices.why: A switch reads to layer 2 and the decision lives at layer 3.

choices.text: It carries no address of its own, so there is no address it could put in the packet
choices.why: Having no address is true and is not what prevents it here.

choices.text: Switches carry traffic in one direction, so a reply would have no path back
choices.why: Traffic runs both ways through a switch, which is how a conversation works.

prompt: How many layers does the model your machine is actually running have?
hint: Not the published one.

prompt: A frame arrives at the server. Put the unwrapping in order.
hint: The outermost envelope comes off first.
items: The card checks the frame is addressed to it, and undamaged
The internet layer checks the address is its own
Transport checks the port and puts the pieces in order
The program is handed the bytes that were sent
trap: It is tempting to put the port check first, because the port is what identifies the program. The port sits inside two envelopes, and both have to come off before anything can read it.

prompt: Why does a small, frequent message cost proportionally more to send than a large one?
hint: The headers are the same size either way.

choices.text: Small messages are held back by transport until enough have gathered to fill a packet
choices.why: Some protocols do delay small writes, and it is not what makes the overhead proportionally larger.

choices.text: The headers are a fixed size, so there is less content behind them
choices.why: Fifty-four bytes of header is most of a keystroke and little of a download.

choices.text: Each layer adds a header sized in proportion to what it was handed
choices.why: Header sizes do not scale with the payload; that is why the ratio moves.

choices.text: The link layer pads anything short up to the largest size the wire allows
choices.why: There is a minimum frame size on some media, and it is nowhere near the maximum.

prompt: A colleague says it is a layer 1 problem. What are they suggesting you look at?
hint: The bottom of the stack.

choices.text: The first program in the chain, since the numbering starts at the application and counts down
choices.why: The numbering starts at the bottom; the application is seven.

choices.text: The cable, the connector or the radio
choices.why: Check the physical thing before anything clever.

choices.text: The address the machine was given, which is the first thing it settles
choices.why: Addresses are layer 3, and getting one is not the first thing that happens.

choices.text: The first router, which is the first device outside the building
choices.why: The number names a layer rather than a position along the path.

prompt: Which description of the horizontal and the vertical movement is right?
hint: One of the two is the conversation and the other is plumbing.

choices.text: Each layer on the way through opens the header below it and hands the contents to the one above
choices.why: Nothing on the way through climbs the stack; that happens at the ends.

choices.text: The two ends exchange one layer at a time, each waiting for the last to be acknowledged
choices.why: The layers are not exchanged in turns; one message carries all the headers at once.

choices.text: Movement up and down happens at the sending machine and not at the far end
choices.why: The far end does the same movement in reverse, which is how it reads anything.

choices.text: The real conversation is between matching layers at the two ends
choices.why: Vertical movement exists to make that horizontal exchange possible.

prompt: A new transport protocol is dropped by some boxes along the path. What explains that?
hint: Somebody reached up into a header they had no business opening.

choices.text: The protocol has to be installed on each router between the ends before it can carry anything
choices.why: Routers read addresses; a transport protocol is not installed in them.

choices.text: Its packets are larger than the wire allows, so they are discarded instead of split
choices.why: Size has a mechanism of its own, and it is not what happens here.

choices.text: It uses a port the operators have not opened, which is settled at the internet layer
choices.why: Ports are a transport matter, and the described box is not a firewall.

choices.text: Those boxes reach up into a header whose shape they assumed
choices.why: A layer violation bought something once and charges for it for twenty years.
